title: Lettre Tate (mai 66) (Cristaux) : lettre (1966), tapuscrit (s.d.), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This page is not Grothendieck's own mathematics. It is page 27 of a typed French text labelled 'n° 380', apparently on Banach algebras. It sits in the folder between Grothendieck's handwritten pages on Hodge–Tate decompositions; the handwritten folio numbers 54 and 55 suggest these sheets were reused as scrap paper. The page develops the holomorphic functional calculus in a unital (Banach) algebra A with unit e.

Proposition 3 (spectral mapping theorem). For f holomorphic near Sp(x), Sp(f(x)) = f(Sp(x)).
- Inclusion f(Sp(x)) ⊂ Sp(f(x)): for t in Sp(x), write f(z) − f(t) = g(z)(z − t) with g holomorphic. The calculus is multiplicative (Propositions 1–2), so f(x) − f(t)e = g(x)(x − te). Since x − te is not invertible and the two factors commute, f(x) − f(t)e is not invertible.
- Reverse inclusion: if t is not in f(Sp(x)), then h = (f − t)^{-1} is holomorphic near Sp(x), and h(x)(f(x) − te) = e.

Corollary. f(x) is invertible if and only if 0 is not in f(Sp(x)).

Proposition 4 (composition rule). (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)). The proof represents holomorphic functions as Cauchy-type integrals against compactly supported measures μ and ρ (e.g. contour measures dz/2πi) supported off the spectrum, in the Waelbroeck style. Thus (g∘f)(x) = ∫ R(x,t) g(f(t)) dρ(t), with R(x,t) the resolvent. The page breaks off just before substituting the Cauchy representation of g, using the fact that f(t) lies in W for t in the support of ρ.

This is standard textbook material (Gelfand–Shilov–Waelbroeck holomorphic functional calculus). It bears no mathematical relation to Grothendieck's surrounding notes on Hodge–Tate decompositions and the Tate letter.
errors: In the formula g(z) = dμ(θ)/(z−θ) the integral sign is missing; it should read g(z) = ∫ dμ(θ)/(z−θ).
Minor: the first inclusion uses commutativity of g(x) and x − te to conclude non-invertibility. This holds because both lie in the closed subalgebra generated by x, but it is not stated explicitly.
Otherwise the arguments are correct and standard.
